lesson.title: Jij, U & Doe Normaal
lesson.subtitle: informal jij versus polite u, and the culture of Dutch directness

hook.title: Two Yous and a Culture
hook.content: Dutch keeps the old thou/you split that English lost: jij is informal singular, u is polite, jullie is plural. Choosing the wrong one is a social statement, not just a grammar mistake.

pattern.title: Jij for peers, u for distance
pattern.content: Jij bent hier (informal), u bent hier (polite), jullie zijn hier (plural). U takes the same verb forms as jij in most of the present tense, but the social meaning is different.
pattern.trap_note: U is not a plural. Jullie is plural; u is polite singular (and can be polite plural in some contexts).

exercises.prompt: Match each English meaning with its Dutch twin (Jij, U & Doe Normaal):
exercises.target_answer: jij, u, jullie, mijn, uw, goedemorgen
exercises.meaning: you (informal singular), you (polite), you (plural), my, your (polite), good morning
exercises.explanation: These are the anchors of "Jij, U & Doe Normaal": read each Dutch form through the pattern, not as a new word.
“Jij bent hier.” is the Dutch form; the other readings bend the pattern of “Jij, U & Doe Normaal”.

cues: The pattern: Jij for peers, u for distance
exercises.explanation: “U bent hier.” puts the thought together the Dutch way — Jij for peers, u for distance.

diagnosis.slip: an English-shaped word order slipped in
diagnosis.cue: U is not a plural. Jullie is plural; u is polite singular (and can be polite plural in some contexts).

exercises.prompt: Which English sentence is built the Dutch way?
exercises.explanation: “Jullie zijn hier.” is word-for-word “You all are here.”. The odd English is the lesson — never a model to produce. Pattern: Jij for peers, u for distance.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
cues: It means: Is this your book?
exercises.explanation: “Is dit uw boek?” reuses only material taught in “Jij, U & Doe Normaal” — Jij for peers, u for distance.
exercises.affirmation: You heard “Is dit uw boek?” — a sentence built from the lesson's own Dutch, practising Jij for peers, u for distance.

twist.prompt: One more, no safety net — say: “What would you like?”
twist.explanation: U takes wilt/wil in the polite register; the question is a service formula.

summary.outcome: Choose jij, u or jullie by register and use the matching possessive.
summary.takeaway: Dutch politeness is a pronoun choice; the verb often looks the same, but the social meaning does not.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on De Brug: Links, Rechts & Rechtdoor.

jij.etymology_derivation: Dutch keeps the old singular thou as jij; English lost it outside dialect and poetry.

u.etymology_derivation: The polite pronoun descends from a title, like German Sie and French vous.

jullie.etymology_derivation: Historically jij plus lui ('people'): a transparent plural you, unlike English.

mijn.etymology_derivation: English mine/my and Dutch mijn are the same possessive.

uw.etymology_derivation: The possessive that belongs to the polite pronoun u.

goedemorgen.etymology_derivation: goed + morgen: the same compound as English good morning.
